page_title: Optimizing a ring buffer for throughput

sources.entry: Optimizing a Ring Buffer for Throughput - Adds cached indices to a single-producer single-consumer ring and shows with counters the coherence traffic removed.

summary.title: Optimizing a ring buffer for throughput
summary.one_liner: Learn how caching the read and write indices in a single-producer single-consumer ring buffer cuts cache-coherency traffic and raises throughput from about 5.5M to 112M items/s.
keywords: how to make a ring buffer faster
takeaways: A classic SPSC ring buffer with cache-line-aligned read and write indices reaches about 5.5M items/s in the author's benchmark on a Ryzen 9 3900X.
Each read/write pair can cause multiple cache line state transitions because the reader and writer keep touching each other's index cache lines.
Keeping a cached copy of the opposite index means the other thread's atomic is only reloaded when the cached value says the queue looks full or empty.
With cached indices the author measured 112M items/s and cache misses dropping from about 350M to 15M.
Further gains are possible with batched push/pop and huge pages to reduce TLB misses.
summary.summary: The article starts with a simple C++ SPSC ring buffer using std::atomic read and write indices, each aligned to a 64-byte cache line, and explains the acquire/release push and pop operations. It benchmarks 100M items through a 100k-slot buffer across two threads on different CCXs using perf counters, reaching about 5.5M ops/s with roughly 3 cache misses per item. The author then explains the MESI-related coherency traffic behind those misses and adds cached copies of the opposite index to the producer and consumer, which raises throughput to about 112M ops/s. It closes with notes on batching and huge pages as further options.
